title: Server logs on Vercel, Supabase and Cloudflare
summary: When the browser only says 500, follow the request hop by hop through the logs of each platform until one of them names the cause.
youWillLearn: Why a 500 is never explained in the browser, and where the explanation lives
Where to find logs in Vercel, Supabase and Cloudflare, and what each one can tell you
How to write log lines you can actually search
What must never end up in a log

glossary.Cloudflare: A service that sits in front of a website, passes good traffic on, and blocks attacks and bots.
glossary.app server: A computer that runs the app's own code and answers the browser. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.database: A program built to store data safely and find it again fast. Notely's is Postgres, run by Supabase.
glossary.log: A line of text a program writes down while it runs, with a timestamp, so you can read later what happened.
glossary.runtime logs: Logs written while your live code handles real requests, as opposed to logs written while the app was being built.
glossary.build logs: The output of turning your code into a deployment: installing packages, compiling, bundling. A failed build never goes live.
glossary.structured logging: Writing each log line as a small JSON object with fixed fields, so you can filter by a field like noteId instead of reading everything.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall: rules at Cloudflare that block suspicious requests before they reach your app.
glossary.Ray ID: Cloudflare's id for one request. It appears on Cloudflare error pages and in the cf-ray response header.
glossary.environment variable: A setting, such as an API key, that the platform hands to your app when it starts, instead of it being written in the code.
glossary.PII: Personally identifiable information: names, emails, addresses, or content a user wrote. Treat it as private.

steps.title: Notely in production, with Cloudflare in front
body: Notely is live. Maya's browser (the screen she uses) sends each request first to Cloudflare, a service in front of the app that blocks bad traffic, then to the app server: Notely's code, running on Vercel.
The app server loads notes from the database, run by Supabase, and asks the Claude API, Anthropic's AI, for summaries.

scene.caption: A request passes Cloudflare, reaches the app server, which uses the database and the Claude API.

steps.title: The browser only knows it was a 500
body: On the live site, Maya's summary fails. DevTools' Network panel shows the request came back 500: the server broke. The response body explains nothing.
That is on purpose. Live servers do not send error details to browsers, because they can reveal secrets. The real error was written down on the server side, in a log.
changes: ~ App Server fails; Browser gets a bare 500
~ Status code 200 → 500
~ Suspects 0 → 4: any part behind the browser

scene.caption: Something behind the browser broke. The browser only gets 500.

steps.title: Every hop keeps a diary
body: Each platform on the request's path writes its own logs. Cloudflare logs what it let through or blocked. Vercel logs what your app server printed. Supabase logs the database's queries and logins.
Debugging a 500 means walking that path in order, checking each log at the same moment, until one of them says what broke.

callout.text: Parcel tracking: "left the depot, arrived at the hub, out for delivery". When a parcel goes missing, you find the last scan that worked and the first one that did not.

changes: ~ Cloudflare, App Server, Database: each keeps its own logs
~ Claude API fades back

scene.caption: Three platforms, three sets of logs. Read them in the order the request travelled.

steps.title: Vercel: what your app server printed
body: In your Vercel project, the Logs tab shows runtime logs: one row per request, with address, status and time. Filter by 5xx. Expand a row to see everything that request printed, including errors and their stack traces.
Build logs are separate. Look there when a deploy fails, not when a request does.

callout.text: Platforms keep runtime logs only for a limited time, shorter on free plans. For a client app, send them to a log service so last week's incident is still readable.

changes: ~ App Server in focus: Vercel's Logs tab
~ Browser, Cloudflare and Database fade back

scene.caption: Start at your own code: the app server's runtime logs.

steps.title: Write log lines you can search
body: A log only helps if the right line exists. Log where a step starts and how it ends, with the ids you would search for: which note, which user.
Structured logging means one small JSON object per line. Then you can filter for "noteId":"n_81" and see that note's whole story.

code.caption: Ids and outcomes, not content. The note's text never goes into the log.

changes: ~ App Server writes a start and an end line per request

scene.caption: Each request now leaves a start line and an end line, tagged with the note's id.

steps.title: Supabase: queries, logins and its API
body: Supabase's dashboard has a Logs section split by source. API: every call to the database, with its status. Postgres: database errors, such as a refused row. Auth: sign-ins, wrong passwords, expired links.
If your app server's log says "Supabase returned an error", this is where the database says why.
changes: ~ Database in focus: API, Postgres and Auth logs
~ App Server steps back

scene.caption: Supabase keeps separate logs for its API, the database and logins.

steps.title: Cloudflare: the request that never arrived
body: Cloudflare sits in front of everything. If a WAF rule or a bot check blocks a request, it never reaches Vercel, so the app server has no log line at all.
A user sees an error but Vercel's logs are empty? Check Cloudflare's security events. Its error pages show a Ray ID you can search for.

callout.text: A Cloudflare error page with a code from 520 to 524 means Cloudflare could not get a good answer from Vercel. The request did leave Cloudflare, so check Vercel's logs at the same time.

changes: ~ Cloudflare in focus: it can block a request
~ Database and App Server fade back

scene.caption: A request blocked at Cloudflare leaves a trace there only. The app server never sees it.

steps.title: Maya's 500, hop by hop
body: Cloudflare: the request passed. Database: the note loaded fine. App Server: summary:failed, Claude API 401. The Claude API did not accept the key.
The cause: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, an environment variable, was set only for Vercel's Preview copies (test versions of the site), not for Production, the live one.

callout.text: After adding the key for Production, deploy again. A running deployment keeps the values it started with.

changes: ~ Cloudflare and Database: fine in their logs
~ App Server log: the Claude API answered 401
~ Suspects 4 → 1

scene.caption: Cloudflare and the database are fine. The app server's log points at the Claude API call.

steps.title: Logs are not a safe place for secrets
body: Debug logging tempts you to print everything: req.headers, process.env, the full prompt. Logs are kept for days, readable by the whole team, and often copied to other services.
One console.log(req.headers) writes users' login cookies to disk. A logged prompt writes their private notes. Log ids and outcomes, never keys, tokens or PII.

callout.text: After Claude Code adds logging, search the diff for headers, process.env, token, prompt and body. Ask it to log ids and status codes instead, and to remove temporary debug logs once the bug is fixed.

changes: ~ App Server: a careless line logs cookies
~ Cloudflare, Database and Claude API fade back

scene.caption: A careless log line copies secrets and private notes into a place many people can read.

steps.title: Recap: follow the request
body: A 500 is explained on the server, never in the browser. Walk the path in order: Cloudflare (blocked?), Vercel's runtime logs (what did my code print?), Supabase's logs (what did the database say?).
Log the start and end of each step with ids, as JSON. Never log secrets or user content. Here, adding the key and redeploying fixed Maya's summary.
changes: ~ Status code 500 → 200: key added, app redeployed
~ Suspects 1 → 0
~ Every part back to normal

scene.caption: Every hop is fine again, and each one keeps a log you know how to read.

quiz.question: Users report an error page, but Vercel's runtime logs show no requests at that time. What is the most likely place to look?

options.why: An error page is a page request. It goes through Cloudflare to Vercel, not straight to Supabase. If Vercel saw nothing, the request stopped before it.

options.text: Cloudflare's security events, since the request may have been blocked before it reached Vercel.
options.why: Cloudflare sits in front. A blocked request leaves a trace only there, often with a Ray ID shown on the user's error page.

options.text: The browser Console, since the server is clearly fine.
options.why: No log is not the same as fine. It means the request never got there, so look at the step before.

quiz.question: Claude Code adds console.log("request", req.headers, body) to debug a route. What do you ask it to change?

options.text: Nothing, since logs are private to the project.
options.why: Logs are seen by every team member, kept for days and often sent to other services. Cookies and user content do not belong there.
The level is not the problem. The content is: headers carry cookies and tokens, and the body carries user data.

options.text: Log only ids and outcomes, like noteId and the status, as JSON.
options.why: Ids let you follow one request through the logs without copying secrets or private content into them.

quiz.question: You add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY to Production in Vercel's settings. The live site still fails with 401. Why?

options.text: The running deployment started with the old values. It needs a new deploy.
options.why: Environment variables are read into a deployment when it is created. Redeploy so the new value is used.

options.text: Vercel can only hold one API key per project.
options.why: A project can hold many environment variables, each set per environment.

options.text: The key must also be added to Cloudflare.
options.why: Cloudflare only passes the request on. The key is used by your app server on Vercel when it calls the Claude API.

takeaways: A 500 is explained in the server logs, never in the browser. Go there next.
Walk the request in order: Cloudflare (blocked?), Vercel runtime logs (what did my code print?), Supabase logs (what did the database or Auth say?).
No Vercel log line at all? The request probably never arrived. Check Cloudflare.
Log the start and end of each step as JSON with ids like noteId, so you can filter one request's story.
Never log headers, process.env, tokens or user content.
